l: Celmus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Celmus was described by Pliny as a remarkably wise and moderate young man whose passions made no impression on him, causing him to be changed into adamant. l: Crocus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Crocus was associated with Smilax in stories explaining their transformation into flowers. In one version they were a faithful married couple, while in another Crocus rejected Smilax's advances and both were changed into flowers.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Salmacis, a Naiad who avoids hunting, falls in love with Hermaphroditus when she sees him near her spring. Hermaphroditus rejects her advances, but she hides, waits until he enters the water, and seizes him when he is bathing. The Gods unite their bodies into one two-sexed form after Salmacis prays that they never be separated. Hermaphroditus then asks that men who enter the spring emerge half male, and his parents cause the waters to enervate and soften those who touch them.

l: Salmacis, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Salmacis is a Naiad who does not hunt or practice archery and who spends her time bathing, arranging her hair, resting, and gathering flowers. She falls in love with Hermaphroditus, pursues him despite his resistance, and clings to him in the water until their bodies are united.

l: Hermaphroditus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Hermaphroditus is the son of Mercury and the Cytherean Goddess, and his face shows the features of both parents. He rejects Salmacis, but after she seizes him in the spring, he is united with her and becomes neither wholly male nor wholly female; he then asks his parents to make men who enter the spring become half male.

l: the fountain of Salmacis, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The fountain is a clear pool in Lycia or the neighboring Carians, with no fenny reeds, barren sedge, or sharp-pointed rushes, and with green turf and ever-verdant grass around its edges. Salmacis dwells there, and its waters are later tainted with drugs of ambiguous quality.

l: water of the fountain near Halicarnassus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The waters are clear and pleasant in temperature. After Hermaphroditus's parents grant his request, they are made to cause a man who enters them to emerge half a man and to become effeminate when touched.

l: the transformation of Salmacis and Hermaphroditus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The Gods unite Salmacis and Hermaphroditus after she prays that no time separate them. Their two bodies become one human shape with a twofold form, so that they can be called neither woman nor boy, and seem both and neither.

l: the fountain's enervating power, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The fountain is infamous because it enervates with its enfeebling waters and softens the limbs bathed in it. The cause is unknown, but its properties are well known, and the waters acquire this power after Hermaphroditus's parents taint them with drugs of ambiguous quality.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The unit describes Caria, near Halicarnassus, where a fountain was said to change men into women. Their intercourse with the colonists civilized them but also corrupted them through the introduction of the luxurious manners of Greece. The fountain’s effects may have resulted from a peculiar chemical quality in its water, which supposedly made drinkers soft and effeminate.

l: Caria, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Caria is identified as the region containing a fountain near the town of Halicarnassus. The fountain was associated with the reputed transformation of men into women.

l: Greece, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Greece is presented as the source of luxurious manners that were introduced to the barbarians through their contact with Greek colonists.

l: Halicarnassus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Halicarnassus is the town near which, in Caria, the reputedly transformative fountain was located.

l: Argive colony, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The Argive colony was established near the fountain and drove certain barbarians from the neighborhood.

l: Greek colonists, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Greek colonists encountered the displaced barbarians at the fountain when both groups went there for water. Their intercourse civilized the barbarians but also corrupted them by introducing the luxurious manners of Greece.

l: barbarians, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The barbarians were driven from the neighborhood by the Argive colony and had to repair to the fountain for water. Contact with the Greek colonists polished them and exposed them to the luxurious manners of Greece.

l: the fountain of Salmacis, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The fountain near Halicarnassus in Caria was instrumental in civilizing the barbarians and acquired a reputation for changing men into women. The text suggests that its bad reputation may also have arisen from disgraceful adventures occurring near it.

l: water of the fountain near Halicarnassus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The water of the fountain was used by the displaced barbarians, who went there to obtain it. Its unusual effects were possibly attributed to a peculiar chemical quality.

l: luxurious manners of Greece, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The luxurious manners of Greece were introduced to the barbarians through their intercourse with the Greek colonists. They are described as corrupting the barbarians even while Greek contact civilized them.

l: chemical quality of the water, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: A peculiar chemical quality of the water is proposed as a possible explanation for the fountain’s extraordinary effects. Such a quality might have made those who drank it soft and effeminate.

l: effeminacy caused by the fountain, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The fountain was reputed to make men into women, possibly because its water made drinkers soft and effeminate. This explanation is presented as a possibility rather than a certainty.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Bacchus punishes the daughters of Minyas for despising him and desecrating his festival. Their webs and cloth transform into ivy, vine shoots, and grapes. As dubious night begins, the house fills with shaking, torches, fires, and phantom beasts. The daughters hide and are transformed into small winged creatures that avoid light, fly at night, and frequent houses rather than woods.

l: Bacchus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Bacchus punishes the daughters of Minyas for their contempt of his worship and their desecration of his festival.

l: three daughters of Minyas, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The daughters of Minyas continue working while despising Bacchus and desecrating his festival. They hide throughout the smoking house as fires and light appear, then acquire membranes and wings, lose their former shape, and become small night-flying creatures.

l: festival of Bacchus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Bacchus's festival is desecrated by the daughters of Minyas, whose contempt for it brings punishment.

l: the daughters' work, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The daughters continue their work when the strange transformation begins. Their work is associated with webs and cloth that become green and produce foliage, vines, and grapes.

l: webs, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The webs begin to grow green and put forth foliage like ivy. Parts of them change into vines, and their former threads become vine shoots.

l: cloth, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The cloth hanging in the loom puts forth foliage like ivy. Its purple color lends splendor to the tinted grapes.

l: ivy, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Ivy foliage grows from the cloth and webs as the transformation begins.

l: vines, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Vines arise from parts of the transformed work, with vine branches springing from the warp.

l: the house, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The house seems to shake as dubious night begins. Unctuous torches burn, the building shines with glowing fires, phantom savage beasts howl, and the daughters hide throughout it while it smokes.

l: dubious night, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Dubious night begins after the day has passed, at a time that can be called neither darkness nor light. It arrives together with the remaining light.

l: darkness, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Darkness accompanies the transformation and prevents the daughters from knowing how they have lost their former shape. The transformed creatures avoid the light and fly abroad by night.

l: light, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Light remains during the beginning of dubious night, while torches and fires illuminate the house. The transformed creatures abhor the light.

l: bats, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The daughters of Minyas are changed into bats, which frequent houses rather than woods and fly at night.

l: transformation of the daughters of Minyas into bats, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The transformation occurs as the daughters hide from fires and light. A membrane stretches over their small limbs, covers their arms with light wings, and leaves them with diminutive squeaking voices; they then fly by night and derive their name from the late evening.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes
s: The footnote explains the names of νυκτερίδες and vespertiliones. νυκτερίδες is the Greek name, derived from νυξ, meaning “night.” vespertiliones is the Latin name, derived from vesper, meaning “evening,” because of their habits.

l: νυκτερίδες, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes
s: νυκτερίδες is the Greek name for them. The name derives from νυξ, meaning “night.”

l: vespertiliones, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes
s: vespertiliones is the Latin name for them. The name derives from vesper, meaning “evening,” because of their habits.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Juno, enraged that Ino prospers through her connection with Bacchus, sends Tisiphone to poison Athamas and Ino with madness. Athamas kills their son Learchus, while Ino flees with Melicerta and throws herself and the child into the sea. At Venus's request, Neptune removes their mortality and transforms Ino into Leucothoë and Melicerta into Palæmon. Juno then transforms Ino's Sidonian attendants into stone and birds when they condemn her severity.

l: Juno, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Juno resents Ino's prosperity, her alliance with Athamas, and her connection with Bacchus. She sends Tisiphone against Athamas and Ino, rejoices at the resulting violence, and transforms Ino's attendants after they reproach her.

l: Tisiphone, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Tisiphone agrees to Juno's command and leaves the infernal realms carrying a bloody torch and wearing a cloak red with blood. She brings snakes and a poisonous mixture to Athamas and Ino, infecting their minds with madness, rage, and murderous intent.

l: Athamas, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Athamas is struck by Tisiphone's poison and becomes mad. Believing that he sees a lioness with two cubs, he pursues Ino and kills Learchus by dashing him against the stones.

l: Ino, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Ino is poisoned by Tisiphone and affected by madness. After Athamas kills Learchus, she flees with Melicerta, calls on Bacchus, and leaps from a rock into the sea; Neptune transforms her into the sea deity Leucothoë.

l: Learchus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Learchus, smiling and reaching his arms from Ino's bosom, is seized by the maddened Athamas. Athamas whirls him through the air and dashes his bones against the hard stones.

l: Melicerta, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Melicerta is carried by Ino as she flees from Athamas and leaps into the sea. Neptune removes his mortality and transforms him into the deity Palæmon.

l: Bacchus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Bacchus's divine power is celebrated throughout Thebes, and Ino, his aunt and foster-mother, proclaims his might. Ino invokes his name while fleeing with Melicerta, which makes Juno mockingly say that her foster-child should perform this service for her.

l: Neptune, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Neptune responds to Venus's request and takes compassion on Ino and Melicerta in the sea. He removes what is mortal from them, changes their names and shapes, and makes them sea deities.

l: Venus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Venus pities Ino and Melicerta after they fall into the sea. She asks Neptune to take them among his deities and appeals to her connection with the sea.

l: Palæmon, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Palæmon is the new divine name given to Melicerta when Neptune transforms him after the fall into the sea.

l: Leucothoë, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Leucothoë is the new divine name given to Ino when Neptune transforms her after the fall into the sea.

l: Sidonian attendants of Ino, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The Sidonian attendants follow Ino's footprints to the edge of the rock and, believing Ino and Melicerta dead, lament the house of Cadmus and reproach Juno. Juno transforms them according to their positions: some become fixed in stone and others become birds that skim over the sea.

l: Palace of Athamas, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Juno desires that the Palace of Athamas and the house of Cadmus should not stand. Tisiphone reaches the palace, where her arrival is marked by terror, shaking door-posts, and paleness on the door.

l: the Molarian rock, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The rock above the sea is worn hollow at its lower part by the waves, while its rugged summit projects over the open sea. Ino climbs it and casts herself and Melicerta into the deep.

l: Juno's poisoning of Athamas and Ino, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Juno's poisoning of Athamas and Ino is carried out by Tisiphone, who throws a mixture of poison, Cerberus's foam, Echidna's venom, rage, tears, crime, and the love of murder into their breasts. The poison attacks their minds rather than their limbs and produces their direful actions.

l: Athamas's killing of Learchus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Athamas's killing of Learchus occurs while Athamas is mad and mistakes Ino and her children for a lioness and her cubs. He seizes Learchus from Ino, whirls him around, and dashes him to pieces against the stones.

l: Ino and Melicerta's transformation into sea deities, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Ino and Melicerta's transformation into sea deities follows their fall from the rock into the sea. At Venus's intercession, Neptune removes their mortality, changes their forms and names, and makes Ino Leucothoë and Melicerta Palæmon.

l: transformation of Ino's attendants, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The transformation of Ino's attendants is imposed by Juno after they blame her for being unjust and too severe. Some attendants become stone in the positions they occupy, while others become birds that skim over the sea.

l: madness, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Madness is brought to Athamas and Ino by Tisiphone's poison. It drives Athamas to kill Learchus and causes Ino to flee with Melicerta and leap into the sea.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The unit explains the myth of Ino, Athamas, and Melicerta, including their family history, conflicts, deaths, and later worship as sea deities. Ino sought to destroy Nephele's children, while Athamas was deceived into believing that the sacrifice of Nephele's children would end the famine at Thebes. Phryxus and Helle escaped by sailing to Colchis, but Athamas later killed Learchus and pursued Ino and Melicerta, who threw themselves into the sea. The explanation identifies Ino and Melicerta with Leucothoë and Palæmon and connects them with later religious practices and festivals.

l: Ino, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Ino was the daughter of Cadmus and the second wife of Athamas. She opposed Nephele's children, caused the seed to be parched during the famine at Thebes, fled with Melicerta from Athamas, and threw herself into the sea. She was later worshipped as the sea deity Leucothoë, and the Romans called her Matuta.

l: Athamas, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Athamas, the son of Æolus and great-grandson of Deucalion, married Ino after divorcing Nephele and later took Ino back after divorcing her in turn. He ordered the oracle of Delphi to be consulted during the famine at Thebes, killed Learchus after discovering Ino's deception, and pursued Ino and Melicerta.

l: Melicerta, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Melicerta was the son of Ino and Athamas and the foster-child of Ino's sister Semele's son, Bacchus. He fled with Ino and was carried with her into the sea, after which he was identified with the sea deity Palæmon and worshipped in Greece and Rome.

l: Learchus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Learchus was the son of Ino and Athamas. Athamas killed him after discovering Ino's deceptive conduct.

l: Nephele, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Nephele was a wife of Athamas before Ino and the mother of Phryxus and Helle. After Nephele was divorced, Athamas took Ino back, and Ino sought to destroy Nephele's children.

l: Phryxus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Phryxus was one of Nephele's children and was warned about Ino's designs. He escaped with Helle by ship and reached Colchis, where Æetes received him kindly.

l: Helle, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Helle was Nephele's daughter and Phryxus's companion in the voyage to Colchis. She fell overboard and was drowned, or died naturally during the passage, and the Hellespont was said to have received its name from her.

l: Thebes, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Thebes was afflicted by a famine during the conflict involving Ino and Athamas. The famine was said to have been caused by Ino, who ordered the seed to be parched before it was sown.

l: the famine at Thebes, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The famine at Thebes was attributed to Ino's order that seed be parched before sowing. Athamas sought an oracle's guidance about it, and the response called for the sacrifice of Nephele's children.

l: the sacrifice of Nephele's children, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The sacrifice of Nephele's children was presented as the means of ending the famine at Thebes. The oracle's message was obtained after the priests were allegedly bribed or the messengers corrupted, but Phryxus was warned and escaped with Helle.

l: Phryxus and Helle's voyage to Colchis, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Phryxus and Helle's voyage to Colchis began when Phryxus was warned of Ino's designs. Phryxus reached Colchis and received a kind welcome from Æetes, while Helle fell from the ship or died during the passage.

l: Ino's suicide, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Ino's suicide occurred when she fled from Athamas after he killed Learchus and pursued her for revenge. Carrying Melicerta, she threw herself from a rock into the sea.

l: Ino and Melicerta's transformation into sea deities, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The transformation of Ino and Melicerta was said to have changed them into sea deities named Leucothoë and Palæmon. The explanation presents this story as a way of consoling their relatives after Ino and Melicerta died.

l: the explanation of the myth, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The explanation of the myth presents the story as possibly based on historical facts reported by Herodotus, Diodorus Siculus, and Pausanias. It connects the deaths and transformations of Ino and Melicerta with their later worship, the Isthmian games, and Roman religious practices.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Cadmus leaves Thebes after the calamities and prodigies affecting his family and wanders with his wife Hermione to Illyria. Remembering the dragon he killed and whose teeth he sowed, Cadmus wishes to become a serpent and is transformed. Hermione laments his change and asks the Gods to transform her as well, after which she becomes a serpent too. The two serpents enter a nearby grove and no longer harm or avoid mankind.

l: Cadmus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Cadmus leaves Thebes because of sorrow, calamities, and prodigies, and reaches Illyria with his exiled wife. He recalls killing the dragon and sowing its teeth, wishes to become a serpent, and is transformed while still trying to speak to his wife.

l: Hermione, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Hermione accompanies Cadmus into exile and wandering and laments as he changes into a serpent. She asks the celestial Gods to transform her likewise and becomes a serpent.

l: Thebes, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Thebes is the city founded by Cadmus, which he leaves because the misfortunes and prodigies connected with his family have driven him away.

l: Illyria, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Illyria is the place whose coast Cadmus reaches after a long series of wandering with his exiled wife.

l: the Gods, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The Gods have made Cadmus's daughter and little grandson deities of the sea. Cadmus wonders whether their care avenges the dragon's death, and Hermione appeals to the celestial Gods to transform her into a serpent.

l: dragon, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The dragon was pierced and killed by Cadmus's spear after he left Sidon. Cadmus sowed its teeth in the ground as an unknown seed and later wonders whether it was sacred.

l: Cadmus and Hermione as serpents, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Cadmus and Hermione become two serpents and enter the covert of an adjacent grove in joined folds. They do not shun mankind or wound people, and they retain memory of what they once were.

l: Cadmus's exile and wandering, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Cadmus is forced to leave Thebes and wanders for a long time with his exiled wife. Their wandering ends when they reach the coast of Illyria.

l: transformation of Cadmus and Hermione into serpents, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Cadmus's body lengthens, develops scales and azure spots, and loses its human form as he becomes a serpent. Hermione then undergoes a similar transformation after asking the Gods for it, and the two enter a nearby grove together.

l: the calamities of Cadmus's family, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The calamities of Cadmus's family, together with sorrow and numerous prodigies, drive him from Thebes. While in Illyria, Cadmus and Hermione recount the misfortunes of their house.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes
s: Cadmus was driven from the throne of Thebes after a conspiracy and retired with his wife Hermione into Illyria. He commanded the Illyrian army, became king, and assisted the Enchelians in their war against the Illyrians. The story that Cadmus and Hermione became serpents was later invented, possibly from associations among the Phoenicians, the word for serpent, and the Illyrians. Various writers also proposed alternative explanations for Cadmus's name and origin.

l: Cadmus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes
s: After a conspiracy drove him from the throne of Thebes, Cadmus retired with Hermione into Illyria. He commanded the Illyrian army, was chosen king, and assisted the Enchelians in their war against the Illyrians; the story of his transformation after death was later invented.

l: Hermione, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes
s: Hermione was Cadmus's wife and retired with him into Illyria. The story later claimed that she and Cadmus became serpents.

l: Illyria, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes
s: Illyria was the place where Cadmus and Hermione retired after leaving Thebes. Cadmus commanded its army, became king, and died there according to the explanation.

l: transformation of Cadmus and Hermione into serpents, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes
s: The transformation was presented as a story invented after Cadmus's death. It may have arisen from the Phoenician word Chiva, possibly meaning serpent, and from the Greeks' association of the Illyrians with serpents or basilisks.

l: Phœnicians, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes
s: The Phoenicians were anciently called Achivi, a name they retained after establishing themselves in Greece. Their possible word Chiva for serpent was proposed as part of the explanation for the story about Cadmus and Hermione.

l: serpent, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes
s: Chiva was identified as a Hebrew and perhaps Phoenician word for serpent. The Greeks also called the ancient inhabitants of Illyria serpents and basilisks.

l: Greeks, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes
s: The Greeks reportedly said after Cadmus's death that Cadmus and Hermione were serpents, possibly because of Cadmus's Phoenician origin. They also called the Illyrians serpents and basilisks.

l: Phoenician origin of Cadmus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes
s: Cadmus's Phoenician origin was proposed as a basis for the story that he and Hermione became serpents. Bochart connected the name Cadmus with Cadmonia, the eastern part of Phoenicia.

l: Enchelians, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes
s: The Enchelians received Cadmus's assistance in their war against the Illyrians. After the Illyrians were defeated, they gave the crown to Cadmus.

l: Illyrians, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes
s: The Illyrians were defeated by the Enchelians with Cadmus's assistance and gave their crown to Cadmus to obtain peace. They were also associated by the Greeks with serpents and basilisks.

l: war between the Enchelians and Illyrians, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes
s: Cadmus assisted the Enchelians in their war against the Illyrians. The Illyrians were defeated, and they gave the crown to Cadmus in order to obtain peace.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Perseus, son of Jupiter and Danaë, carries Medusa’s head across Africa and Libya, where its bloody drops produce serpents. He travels to Atlas’s kingdom and asks for hospitality, but Atlas remembers an oracle that a son of Jupiter will take his golden fruit and drives Perseus away. Perseus exposes the Gorgon’s head, transforming Atlas into a mountain that supports the heavens. Acrisius regrets denying that Perseus and Bacchus are descended from Jupiter.

l: Perseus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Perseus, the son of Jupiter and Danaë, carries Medusa’s head through Africa and across the world. He asks Atlas for hospitality, but when Atlas threatens him, Perseus exposes the Gorgon’s head and transforms Atlas into a mountain.

l: Jupiter, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Jupiter is identified as the father of Perseus and as the ancestor of Bacchus. Acrisius first denies that Perseus is Jupiter’s offspring, but later regrets not acknowledging his grandson.

l: Medusa, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Medusa is killed by Perseus. Her head is carried by Perseus, and bloody drops from it produce various serpents when they fall upon the ground.

l: Gorgon’s head, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The Gorgon’s head is the memorable spoil carried by Perseus after his victory. When Perseus exposes it to Atlas, its horrible features transform Atlas into a mountain.

l: Atlas, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Atlas, the son of Iapetus and king of the country, possesses an orchard with golden fruit guarded by a huge dragon. Remembering an oracle, he refuses Perseus hospitality and attempts to drive him away, but Perseus exposes the Gorgon’s head and changes him into a mountain.

l: Perseus's killing of Medusa, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Perseus's killing of Medusa enables him to carry the Gorgon’s head as a spoil. Blood from the head falls onto the Libyan sands, where the ground quickens it into various serpents.

l: Atlas's transformation, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Atlas's transformation occurs when Perseus exposes the Gorgon’s head to him. Atlas’s beard and hair become woods, his shoulders and hands become mountain ridges, his head becomes the mountain’s summit, and his bones become stones.

l: the oracle concerning Atlas's golden fruit, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The oracle given by the Parnassian Themis foretells that Atlas’s tree will be stripped of its gold and that a son of Jupiter will receive the prize. Because Atlas fears this prophecy, he encloses the orchard and expels strangers from his territories.

l: golden apples, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The golden fruit grows on trees whose leaves and branches shine with gold. Atlas fears that it will be taken by a son of Jupiter, as foretold by the oracle.

l: Atlas's mountain form, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: In Atlas's mountain form, his woods, ridges, stones, and summit make up an immense mountain. The whole heaven, with its many stars, rests upon him.

l: Acrisius, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Acrisius was the son of Abas, king of Argos, and the father of Danaë. After hearing a prediction that Danaë’s child would kill him, he confined her in a tower or subterraneous chamber, but later exposed her and Perseus in a boat.

l: Danaë, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Danaë was the daughter of Acrisius and the mother of Perseus. Acrisius confined her to prevent her from bearing the child foretold to kill him, but she was reached either by Jupiter in myth or, in one rationalizing account, by her uncle Prœtus through bribed guards.

l: Jupiter, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Jupiter was said to be the father of Perseus by Danaë, having seduced her in the form of a shower of gold. He was also identified as the father of Bacchus and an ancestor of Acrisius through Belus.

l: Perseus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Perseus was the son of Danaë and Jupiter, and Acrisius’s predicted killer. l: Gorgons, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The Gorgons were variously described as female warriors near Lake Tritonis, savage women living in caves and forests, wealthy sisters who owned islands and a golden statue, beautiful women whose appearance turned people into statues, or a deadly animal called a gorgon. They were said to inhabit the Gorgades in the Æthiopian Sea, possibly the Cape Verde Islands.

l: Medusa, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Medusa was described by Pausanias as a ruler who laid waste to neighboring lands and was killed by Perseus. Other interpretations present her as one of three wealthy sisters, a beautiful woman, or the source of the story of the petrifying Gorgon head.

l: Danaë’s seduction by Jupiter, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The myth says that Jupiter seduced Danaë in the form of a shower of gold. One ancient rationalization instead identifies Prœtus, Danaë’s uncle, as the man who gained access to her tower by corrupting the guards with gold.

l: Perseus's birth, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Perseus was born to Danaë after her confinement by Acrisius. Acrisius then exposed Danaë and Perseus in a boat, but they survived after reaching Seriphus, where Polydectes received them.

l: Perseus's killing of Medusa, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: In the myth, Perseus killed Medusa and took her head. In Pausanias’s account, Perseus and companions surprised Medusa and her escort by night; in another interpretation, he killed Medusa after seizing the common minister of her sisters and obtaining their golden statue.

l: Gorgon’s head, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The myth says that Medusa’s head turned those who looked upon it into stone. One interpretation explains this as the terror produced by Perseus’s fame and by the Gorgon statue or its head, which he placed on the prow of his ship.

l: Perseus myth interpretations, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The unit presents rationalizations of Perseus’s birth, his killing of Medusa, the petrifying power of Medusa’s head, the transformation of Atlas, Pegasus, and the golden apples. These interpretations connect the myths with political events, military exploits, voyages, geography, wealth, animals, and distinctive natural products.

l: Gorgon myth interpretations, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The Gorgon myths are interpreted as accounts of female warriors, savage women, wealthy sisters with a shared minister, beautiful women whose appearance caused astonishment, or a deadly animal. l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Perseus reaches Æthiopia and rescues Andromeda from a sea monster after finding her chained to a rock as punishment for her mother's boast. He kills the monster, marries Andromeda, and places Medusa's head on sea plants, which become coral. At the wedding feast, Perseus recounts how he beheaded Medusa and explains that Minerva transformed Medusa's hair into serpents after Neptune violated her in Minerva's temple.

l: Perseus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Perseus flies to Æthiopia after Atlas has been changed into a mountain. He kills the sea monster threatening Andromeda, marries her, and later recounts how he beheaded Medusa and obtained the Gorgon's head.

l: Atlas transformed into a mountain, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Atlas has been changed into a mountain before Perseus proceeds to Æthiopia.

l: Ethiopia, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Æthiopia is the land where Perseus finds Andromeda exposed on a rock and where Cepheus and Cassiope rule.

l: Cepheus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Cepheus is Andromeda's father. He and Cassiope mourn Andromeda's danger, agree to Perseus's marriage condition, promise a kingdom as her dowry, and welcome Perseus as their son-in-law and the preserver of their house.

l: Andromeda, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Andromeda is found with her arms bound to a rock, awaiting the sea monster because of her mother's boast about beauty. Perseus rescues her, and she becomes his wife.

l: Cassiope, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Cassiope is Andromeda's mother, whose confidence in her beauty leads to Andromeda's punishment. She mourns at the rock and later rejoices when Perseus rescues Andromeda and becomes her son-in-law.

l: Andromeda's exposure to the sea monster, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Andromeda is bound to a hard rock and exposed to the approaching sea monster as punishment for her mother's boast. Her parents can bring her only tears, lamentations, and embraces until Perseus intervenes.

l: sea monster, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The sea monster rises from the ocean and advances on Andromeda. Perseus wounds it repeatedly with his sword, finally killing it by thrusting the sword through its entrails.

l: Perseus's rescue of Andromeda, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Perseus offers to save Andromeda in exchange for marriage, then attacks the sea monster from the air and kills it. Andromeda is released from her chains and becomes the reward and cause of his labor.

l: nuptials of Perseus and Andromeda, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Perseus and Andromeda marry after the rescue without a dowry. Hymenaeus and Cupid lead the wedding celebration, and the marriage is honored with music, perfumes, garlands, and a feast.

l: Gorgon’s head, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Perseus carries the snake-bearing Gorgon's head and places it face-down on sea plants softened by leaves. He later explains that he cut it from Medusa's neck while she slept.

l: Medusa, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Medusa is the Gorgon whose face turns men and beasts to stone. Perseus sees her reflection in his shield, beheads her while she sleeps, and says that Pegasus and his winged brother sprang from her blood.

l: coral, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Coral becomes hard when exposed to air. It retains the nature of a sea plant that turns to stone outside the sea after contact with Medusa's head.

l: transformation of sea plants into coral, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Sea plants placed beneath Medusa's head absorb its poison and harden. The sea Nymphs repeat the experiment, and the text says that plants in the sea become coral when removed from it and exposed to air.

l: Minerva, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Perseus dedicates an altar and sacrifices a cow to Minerva. Minerva is said to have changed Medusa's hair into snakes after Neptune violated Medusa in Minerva's temple.

l: Gorgons, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The Gorgons dwell in a remote, fortified place beneath Atlas. Perseus reaches their abode and sees statues of people and wild beasts turned to stone by the sight of Medusa.

l: Medusa's beheading, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Perseus beheads Medusa while she and her serpents are held in sleep. He accomplishes this by viewing her face through the reflection on the bronze shield carried in his left hand.

l: Medusa's serpents, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Medusa's serpents are mingled with her hair and sleep with her when Perseus attacks. They remain displayed on the front of her breast to terrify her enemies.

l: Medusa's transformation of hair into serpents, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Medusa's hair is transformed into hideous snakes by Minerva. The transformation occurs after Neptune violates Medusa in Minerva's temple, and the snakes become a source of terror to Medusa's foes.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The notes explain details of Perseus’s rescue of Andromeda, his encounter with the sea monster, and his slaying of Medusa. l: Andromeda, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Andromeda is identified as the daughter of Cepheus and Cassiope. She is exposed to be devoured by the sea monster, but Perseus rescues her.

l: Perseus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Perseus uses a reflecting shield associated with Minerva to see Medusa without being seen, cuts off Medusa’s head, and escapes her pursuing sisters. He later rescues Andromeda from the approaching sea monster.

l: Medusa, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Medusa is slain by Perseus, who seizes her by the hair while viewing her reflection in the shield and cuts off her head. Pegasus and Chrysaor are said to have sprung from her blood.

l: sea monster, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The sea monster is sent by Neptune at the request of the Nereids against the Ethiopians. Jupiter Ammon’s oracle declares that Andromeda must be exposed to it, and Perseus confronts and rescues her from it.

l: Andromeda's exposure to the sea monster, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The exposure of Andromeda is presented as a response to Cassiope’s comparison of her beauty with that of the Nereids. One proposed interpretation is that it reflects Andromeda’s forced betrothal to a fierce pirate prince in exchange for the safety of Cepheus’s realms.

l: Perseus's killing of Medusa, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The slaying of Medusa involves Perseus using a reflecting shield from Minerva, taking Medusa by the hair, and cutting off her head while avoiding direct sight of her. l: interpretation of the Andromeda myth, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The explanation proposes that the Andromeda story may preserve an account of a pirate prince, a forced betrothal, and Perseus’s defeat of the pirate. It also suggests that Phineus may have been the enemy from whom Andromeda was rescued, or that the sea monster may have been the name of the ship intended to carry her away.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE FIFTH.
s: While Perseus relates his adventures, Phineus attacks him at the wedding feast because Andromeda had previously been promised to Phineus. Cepheus defends Perseus and explains that Perseus saved Andromeda from the sea monster, while Perseus fights Phineus and his numerous followers with help from Pallas. When Perseus displays the Gorgon head, many attackers and some of his own soldiers become stone, and he finally petrifies Phineus. Perseus then enters his native city with Andromeda and attacks the usurper Prœtus.

l: Perseus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE FIFTH.
s: Perseus is attacked by Phineus and his followers during the wedding feast. He fights them with great valor, kills or wounds many enemies, and uses the Gorgon head when their numbers threaten to overwhelm him. He later petrifies Phineus and enters his native city with Andromeda to attack Prœtus.

l: Phineus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE FIFTH.
s: Phineus attacks Perseus because Andromeda, his former betrothed, has been given to Perseus. He leads a large force against Perseus but eventually begs for his life after seeing his followers turned to stone. Perseus turns him into a stone statue, preserving his fearful and supplicant expression.

l: Andromeda, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE FIFTH.
s: Andromeda is identified as Phineus’s former betrothed and Perseus’s new wife. Her father, Cepheus, says that Perseus saved her from being sacrificed to the sea monster. She later enters Perseus’s native city with him.

l: Cepheus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE FIFTH.
s: Cepheus rebukes Phineus for attacking Perseus and argues that Perseus earned Andromeda by saving her life. He calls the disturbance contrary to his will and invokes justice, good faith, and the gods of hospitality before leaving the house.

l: Medusa, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE FIFTH.
s: Medusa is referred to as the source of the head that Perseus uses as a weapon. Perseus’s falchion had previously been proved in Medusa’s slaughter.

l: Gorgon’s head, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE FIFTH.
s: Perseus produces the Gorgon head when he is surrounded by Phineus and a thousand followers. Those who look toward it become immovable stone, including many of Phineus’s men and eventually Phineus himself.

l: Medusa’s petrifying gaze, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE FIFTH.
s: The petrifying power associated with Medusa’s gaze turns people who behold the Gorgon head into stone. It affects enemies and also accidentally petrifies Aconteus, a soldier fighting for Perseus.

l: Phineus’s attack, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE FIFTH.
s: Phineus’s attack begins when he rushes into the palace with his adherents and attempts to kill Perseus. His spear misses Perseus and kills Rhœtus instead, after which the fighting spreads throughout the wedding feast.

l: battle at the wedding feast, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE FIFTH.
s: The wedding celebration becomes a violent battle between Perseus and Phineus’s followers. Numerous combatants are killed by swords, spears, and improvised weapons, while Pallas protects and encourages Perseus. The battle ends when Perseus displays the Gorgon head and petrifies many of the combatants.

l: petrification of Phineus and his followers, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE FIFTH.
s: Perseus petrifies Phineus’s followers by making them behold the Gorgon head; two hundred remaining bodies become rigid stone. Phineus recognizes his petrified friends, begs Perseus to remove the head, and is then turned into a stone statue himself.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The notes explain that the story of Andromeda may have taken place in Æthiopia, but is more probably associated with the coast of Africa near Joppa. Josephus, Strabo, Pomponius Mela, and Pliny connect the event with Joppa and describe local traditions about Andromeda’s chains, the royal family, and the monster. The explanation interprets Perseus’s power to turn enemies to stone as a metaphor for his heroism and the terror caused by his victory over the Gorgons. It also suggests that the alleged metamorphoses into stone may have arisen from the rocky nature of Seriphus or from reports about Medusa’s head.

l: Cepheus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Cepheus is identified as the father of Andromeda and, according to Pomponius Mela, as king of Joppa. The memory of Cepheus and his brother Phineus was reportedly honored at Joppa with religious services.

l: Andromeda, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Andromeda is the central figure in the story associated by some writers with Æthiopia and by others with the coast of Africa near Joppa. Josephus reportedly said that the marks of the chains with which she was fastened remained on a rock in his time.

l: Perseus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Perseus is described as having an alleged power to turn his enemies into stone by showing them the Gorgon’s head. The explanation treats this power as a metaphor for his heroism and for the terror produced by his victory over the Gorgons.

l: Ethiopia, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Æthiopia is proposed by some as the setting of the story of Andromeda. The explanation considers the coast of Africa a more probable location.

l: Joppa, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Joppa, or Jaffa, is identified by Josephus and Strabo as the place near which the event involving Andromeda occurred. Pomponius Mela calls Cepheus its king and says that its inhabitants honored Cepheus and Phineus and displayed the bones of the monster.

l: Medusa, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Medusa is connected with the stories of petrifying enemies through the Gorgon’s head. The explanation suggests that reports of Perseus turning enemies to stone may have derived from the terror associated with Medusa’s head.

l: Gorgon’s head, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The Gorgon’s head is said to have been the means by which Perseus allegedly petrified his enemies. The explanation presents this as a metaphorical account of the fear caused by his victories.

l: sea monster, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The monster was said to have been destined to devour Andromeda. Pomponius Mela and Pliny report that the inhabitants of Joppa displayed its bones, while Vossius suggests that the story may refer to the Syrian god Dagon, represented as a fish or sea-monster.

l: story of Andromeda, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The story of Andromeda is placed by some accounts in Æthiopia, but the explanation considers the coast of Africa near Joppa more likely. It concerns Andromeda’s fastening to a rock and the monster that was supposed to devour her.

l: alleged metamorphoses into stone, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The alleged metamorphoses into stone are explained as stories arising from Perseus’s reputed use of the Gorgon’s head against his enemies. Bochart further supposes that the rocky character of Seriphus helped produce these traditions.

l: heroism of Perseus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The heroism of Perseus is presented as the probable reality behind the claim that he could turn enemies into stone. His fame and victories were said to create such consternation that the metaphor was reported as a literal power.

l: victory over the Gorgons, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The victory over the Gorgons is said to have caused widespread terror and to have contributed to reports that Perseus could petrify his enemies by displaying the Gorgon’s head.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Polydectes continues to deny Perseus’s victory over Medusa, so Perseus turns him to stone with Medusa’s face. Minerva leaves Seriphus and visits the Muses at Mount Helicon, where she learns about Pegasus, the fountain he created, and Pyreneus’s failed attempt to assault the Muses. The Muses also tell Minerva how the nine Pierides challenged them to a singing contest and were transformed into magpies after losing. Calliope then prepares to sing for the contest.

l: Polydectes, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Polydectes, ruler of Seriphus, continues to hate Perseus and claims that Perseus’s victory over Medusa is a fiction. Perseus answers by using Medusa’s face to turn Polydectes into stone.

l: Perseus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Perseus is still regarded as having endured many toils and sorrows, though Polydectes denies his achievements. Perseus proves the truth of Medusa’s death by turning Polydectes to stone with Medusa’s face.

l: Medusa, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Medusa’s face is used by Perseus as proof that her death was real. Its power turns Polydectes into stone without blood.

l: Perseus's killing of Medusa, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Polydectes calls the death of Medusa a fiction, but Perseus demonstrates its reality by using Medusa’s face to petrify him.

l: Minerva, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Minerva leaves Seriphus, passing with Cythnus and Gyarus on her right, and travels toward Mount Helicon. She visits the Muses, admires the fountain and its surroundings, and listens to their account of Pyreneus and the Pierides.

l: Helicon, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Mount Helicon is the destination to which Minerva travels to visit the Muses. It contains their habitation, sacred streams, groves, caves, and flower-covered grass.

l: Muses, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The Muses welcome Minerva at Mount Helicon and show her the fountain produced by Pegasus. They tell her how Pyreneus threatened them and how the Pierides challenged them to a singing contest.

l: Pegasus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Pegasus is described as the winged steed sprung from the blood of Medusa. His hard hoof opened the new fountain at Mount Helicon.

l: fountain of Pegasus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The fountain of Pegasus was opened by the hard hoof of Pegasus, who sprang from the blood of Medusa. Minerva visits it and admires its waters.

l: Pyreneus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Pyreneus had seized Daulian and Phocean land with Thracian troops and unjustly ruled it. He invited the Muses into his house during a storm, then attempted violence, but they escaped by taking wing.

l: death of Pyreneus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: After the Muses flew away, Pyreneus climbed onto the top of his house and tried to follow them. He threw himself from the tower, fell on his face, and broke the bones of his skull, dying in his own blood.

l: magpies, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The magpies are nine birds that imitate everything and speak with distinct human-like voices. They are the transformed Pierides and remain perched on lofty branches while lamenting their fate.

l: Pierides, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The Pierides are nine sisters, daughters of Pierus and Evippe, who challenged the Muses to a contest of voice and skill. After being defeated, they increased the number of the birds by becoming magpies.

l: contest between the Muses and the Emathian sisters, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The Pierides challenged the Muses to sing, with the Nymphs serving as judges and the contestants agreeing to withdraw from their lands if defeated. One of the Pierides first sang about the Gods’ flight from Typhoeus, after which the Muses were called upon to answer.

l: Calliope, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Calliope is chosen to manage the Muses’ part of the contest. She rises with her hair gathered in ivy, tunes the lyre, and prepares to sing.

l: song of Calliope, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Calliope’s song begins after she tunes the sounding chords of the lyre. The text states that she sings in concert with the strings, but does not yet give the song’s content.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The notes describe Polydectes, king of Seriphus, who desired Danaë and demanded that Perseus bring him Medusa’s head; Perseus later turned Polydectes to stone after finding Danaë and Dictys seeking refuge. l: Polydectes, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Polydectes was king of Seriphus and became enamored of Danaë while preparing to marry Hippodamia. He demanded that Perseus obtain the head of Medusa, but when Perseus returned and found Danaë and Dictys taking refuge from Polydectes’ violence, he changed Polydectes into stone.

l: Perseus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Perseus was taken with his mother Danaë to Polydectes’ kingdom by Dictys. He was required to bring Polydectes the head of Medusa, returned victorious, and turned Polydectes into stone after finding his mother and Dictys seeking refuge at the altars of the Deities.

l: Muses, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The Muses are associated with Helicon, which was produced by a blow from Pegasus’s hoof, and with Urania, who presided over Astronomy. They are called Mnemonides because they were said to be the daughters of Jupiter and Mnemosyne, and Aonides because of Aonia.

l: Pierus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Pierus is described as a very bad poet whose works contained stories injurious to the credit of the Gods. The explanation suggests that the transformation of his daughters into magpies represented the idle, tiresome, and unmeaning character of his narratives.

l: Pierides, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes

l: Pyreneus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes

l: learning, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes

l: the Muses' adventure with Pyreneus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The adventure is interpreted by Plutarch as a metaphor for Pyreneus’s opposition to learning. The associated story says that the Muses asked the Gods for wings to save themselves and that Pyreneus lost his life pursuing them.

l: the challenge given by the Pierides to the Muses, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The challenge is said not to appear in any writer before Ovid. It is explained through the claim that Pierus was a poor poet whose irreverent and meaningless stories became associated with his daughters’ transformation into magpies.

l: Ovid, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Ceres is praised as the first to plough the earth, provide corn and wholesome food, and establish laws. l: Ceres, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Ceres is credited with first turning the earth with the crooked plough, giving corn and wholesome food to the earth, and establishing laws. Everything is described as the gift of Ceres, who is worthy of song as a goddess.

l: Sicily, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Trinacria is heaped upon the limbs of Typhœus and keeps him beneath its heavy mass. Its land includes the places beneath which his hands, legs, and head are pressed.

l: Typhœus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Typhœus is a giant who once hoped to reach the abodes of Heaven. Confined beneath Trinacria and Ætna, he repeatedly struggles to rise, casts out sand, vomits flame, and tries to throw off the earth and mountains covering him.

l: Ætna, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Ætna bears down upon Typhœus's head and helps keep him imprisoned beneath the earth.

l: Pluto, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Pluto is the ruler of the shades and the god to whom the last portion of the threefold kingdom fell. Fearing that Typhœus's struggles might split the earth and expose the underworld to daylight, he leaves his dark abode in a chariot drawn by black horses to inspect Sicily.

l: Venus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Erycina sees Pluto wandering while she sits upon her mountain. She embraces Cupid and urges him to shoot Pluto so that she and her son may extend their power over the underworld.

l: Cupid, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Cupid is Erycina's winged son and is said to conquer the gods, including Jupiter and the rulers of the deep. At his mother's direction, he chooses an exceptionally sharp and accurate arrow, bends his bow, and shoots Pluto in the breast.

l: Proserpine, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The daughter of Ceres is described as inclined toward virginity, like Pallas and Diana. Erycina seeks to join her to Pluto, her uncle, to advance their shared rule.

l: Cupid's arrows, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Cupid's arrows are described as weapons by which he conquers all, including the gods. At Erycina's direction, he selects one from his thousand arrows that is especially sharp, unerring, and true to the bow.

l: Pluto's survey of Sicily, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Pluto's survey of Sicily begins after Typhœus's struggles make him fear that the earth may open and expose the trembling ghosts to daylight. Riding in a chariot drawn by black horses, he cautiously examines the foundations of the island and sets aside his fear once he finds no insecure place.

l: Cupid's wounding of Pluto, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Cupid bends his flexible bow by pressing his knee against it and strikes Pluto in the breast with a barbed arrow. The attack follows Erycina's command that Cupid extend their influence over Tartarus.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The unit explains that the ancients often attributed difficult natural phenomena to supernatural causes because they lacked natural-philosophical explanations. Ætna’s flames and violent earth shocks were said to result from the Gods throwing Mount Ætna onto the defeated Giant Typhœus, or, in another account, Enceladus. The giant’s attempts to escape the mountain’s weight were believed to cause volcanic eruptions and earthquakes. The notes also identify Sicily’s three promontories and explain several names associated with the island and its mythology.

l: natural phenomena, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The ancients frequently explained natural phenomena through fabulous or supernatural causes when they could not account for them through natural philosophy.

l: Ætna, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Ætna was often seen emitting flames, and the forces within it were associated with violent shocks in the earth. According to the fable, the Gods threw Mount Ætna onto Typhœus or Enceladus.

l: the Gods, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The Gods defeated the Giant Typhœus, or according to some authors Enceladus, and threw Mount Ætna onto his body.

l: Typhœus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Typhœus was described as a Giant defeated by the Gods and buried beneath Mount Ætna. His attempts to free himself from the mountain’s weight were believed to cause fires and earthquakes.

l: Enceladus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: According to some authors, Enceladus took the place of Typhœus in the story of the defeated giant buried beneath Mount Ætna. His attempts to escape the mountain’s weight were believed to cause fires and earthquakes.

l: volcanic eruptions, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The ancients attributed volcanic eruptions to the struggles of Typhœus or Enceladus beneath Mount Ætna. The explanation notes that Ætna contains sulphur and bituminous matter that could provide a natural source for its eruptions.

l: earthquakes, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Earthquakes were attributed in the fable to the attempts of Typhœus or Enceladus to free himself from Mount Ætna. The explanation instead refers to the forces of Ætna’s internal fires struggling for a vent.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Near Henna, Pluto sees Proserpina gathering flowers, seizes her, and carries her away in his chariot. Cyane tries to block Pluto and objects to the abduction, but Pluto forces a passage, after which Cyane dissolves into the waters of her spring. Ceres searches throughout the lands and seas for Proserpina, lighting pine torches at Mount Etna and traveling from sunrise to sunset. When a boy named Stellio mocks Ceres while she drinks barley liquor, she sprinkles him with it and transforms him into a small, spotted newt.

l: Pluto, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Pluto sees Proserpina gathering flowers near Henna, falls in love with her, and seizes her. He drives her away in his chariot, forces a passage through Cyane's stream by throwing his sceptre into it, and descends toward Tartarus.

l: Proserpine, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Proserpina gathers violets and white lilies near the lake of Pergus when Pluto sees and abducts her. She cries out for Ceres and her companions, and the flowers she has collected fall from her loosened garment.

l: Ceres, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Ceres searches throughout the lands and seas for Proserpina, traveling without rest from sunrise to sunset and carrying pine torches lit at Ætna. After becoming thirsty, she receives barley liquor from an old woman and later transforms the mocking boy Stellio into a small, spotted creature.

l: Cyane, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Cyane, a celebrated Sicilian Nymph, rises from her stream and tries to stop Pluto, arguing that Proserpina should have been asked of Ceres rather than carried away. After Pluto forces his chariot through the stream, Cyane grieves, dissolves into tears, and melts into the waters she had guarded.

l: Stellio, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Stellio is the impudent, bold boy who mocks Ceres while she drinks barley liquor. Ceres sprinkles him with the remaining drink, and he is transformed into a diminutive, spotted creature.

l: Henna, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Henna is the place near which the lake of Pergus and its flower-filled grove are located. Proserpina is abducted there while gathering flowers.

l: newt (Stellio), The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The transformed Stellio has a contracted face, legs in place of arms, a tail, and a body smaller than a small lizard. He bears various spots, flees from the old woman, and seeks a hiding place.

l: abduction of Proserpine, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Pluto abducts Proserpina while she is gathering violets and white lilies near Henna. She cries for Ceres and her companions as Pluto drives her away through lakes, sulfurous pools, and a passage opened toward Tartarus.

l: Cyane's transformation into a fountain, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: After Pluto disregards her attempt to stop him, Cyane grieves for Proserpina and for the violated privileges of her spring. Her limbs and body dissolve until her blood is replaced by pure water and nothing remains that can be grasped.

l: Ceres's search for Proserpina, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Ceres searches for Proserpina throughout all lands and seas, finding no rest and traveling from the rising to the setting of the sun. She carries burning pine torches through the darkness, becomes thirsty from her labor, and reaches a thatched cottage where an old woman gives her barley liquor.

l: transformation of Stellio, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: When Stellio mocks Ceres as she drinks, she sprinkles him with barley mixed with liquor. His face changes, legs replace his arms, a tail appears, and his body contracts into a small, spotted creature resembling a newt.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes

l: Henna, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Henna, also called Enna, is described as lying almost exactly at the center of Sicily and therefore as the island’s navel. l: Sicily, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Sicily is presented as the setting in which Ceres ruled and where Proserpine was traditionally carried away. It is also associated with the worship of Ceres, the Palici, Syracuse, Henna, and the early worship of the mysteries later connected with Eleusis.

l: Ceres, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Ceres is Proserpine’s mother and is associated with Henna, agriculture, corn, the Earth, civil laws, and the preservation of private property. l: Proserpine, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Proserpine, the only daughter of Ceres, was said to have been gathering flowers with her companions when she was carried away. Different accounts place her abduction near Henna, in Attica, in Asia, or on the western coast of Spain, and allegorical interpretation connects her disappearance with grain remaining buried in the earth.

l: Pluto, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Pluto is said to have seized Proserpine and carried her into the Infernal Regions. He is also called Dis, a name connected with the riches dug from the earth, and some interpretations identify the figure in the story with a mortal ruler or with the ruler of a low-lying mining region.

l: Syracuse, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Syracuse is described as a city founded by Archias of the Bacchiadae and as having two harbors. According to the account associated with Henna, Pluto descended into the earth not far from Syracuse, where a lake arose and an annual festival was celebrated.

l: Jupiter, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Jupiter is described in one interpretation as a Titan king who received the west in the partition of the world. In the allegorical explanation, he decided the dispute between Ceres and Pluto, symbolizing the earth’s becoming covered with crops again.

l: Isis, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Isis is identified by Banier as the deity whom the Greeks later confused with Ceres. Her worship was said to have been brought from Egypt to Greece after a famine, and Triptolemus established her worship at Eleusis.

l: Triptolemus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Triptolemus is said to have established the worship of Isis at Eleusis and instituted the mysteries brought from Egypt. In the account of famine in Greece, he helped transmit the agricultural religious practices associated with the goddess.

l: Egypt, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Egypt is said to have supplied corn to Greece during a famine in the reign of Erectheus. Those who went there for grain allegedly returned with the worship of the deity who presided over agriculture and with the mysteries later instituted at Eleusis.

l: Greece, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Greece is described as suffering famine during the reign of Erectheus, prompting a request to Egypt for corn. Ceres later went there in search of Proserpine, and the worship and mysteries associated with agriculture were established or spread there.

l: Eleusis, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Eleusis in Attica is where Ceres rested while searching for Proserpine. It became the place where Triptolemus established the worship associated with Isis and instituted the mysteries brought from Egypt.

l: Epirus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes

l: Aidoneus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Aidoneus is presented as a possible historical ruler of Epirus or king of the Molossians who was later confused with Pluto. The account suggests that he may have ordered pirates to seize Proserpine and carry her toward Epirus.

l: Infernal Regions, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The Infernal Regions are associated with Pluto’s low-lying western kingdom, subterranean mines, and the ancient belief that the region was covered in eternal darkness. Le Clerc’s interpretation instead connects them figuratively with Epirus and its river Acheron.

l: rape of Proserpine, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The rape of Proserpine is treated as a story that may preserve natural philosophy, ancient history, or both. Proposed explanations connect it with the seizure of Proserpine by pirates acting for Aidoneus, the mining regions ruled by Pluto, or the burial of grain beneath the earth.

l: abduction of Proserpine, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The abduction of Proserpine is traditionally placed near Henna, where Pluto was said to emerge from a deep cavern in his chariot. Other accounts place it in Attica, Asia, or Spain, while Le Clerc’s historical explanation says that pirates carried her to the seaside and embarked for Epirus.

l: worship of Ceres, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The worship of Ceres was especially prominent at Henna, where the inhabitants were regarded as her priests. It was later connected with agriculture, the Earth, civil order, and the worship brought from Egypt to Greece.

l: Eleusinian mysteries, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The Eleusinian mysteries are described as rites brought from Egypt and instituted at Eleusis by Triptolemus. The text suggests that these mysteries had already been introduced into Sicily, helping explain the tradition that Ceres came from Sicily to Athens.

l: famine in Greece, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: A famine in Greece during the reign of Erectheus led the Greeks to seek corn from Egypt. The crisis encouraged them to adopt the worship of the agricultural deity and helped form the explanation of Ceres and Proserpine’s story.
